content: The effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives may be reduced when co-administered with certain medications. It is recommended to use a non-hormonal contraceptive method in such cases. Below are specific interactions and recommendations: 1. Nemolizumab: This drug decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by inducing CYP3A4 enzyme activity. Therapy modification or close monitoring is advised. Nemolizumab may also increase CYP enzyme activity by suppressing cytokines, potentially reducing systemic levels of sensitive CYP substrates. Dosage adjustments may be necessary. 2. Neomycin (oral): Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 3. Nevirapine: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 4. Nicardipine: Ethinyl estradiol increases nicardipine levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Nirmatrelvir/Ritonavir: These drugs decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by increasing metabolism, likely through CYP2C9 or CYP1A2 induction. Additional non-hormonal contraceptive methods are recommended for the remainder of the cycle. 6. Nitrofurantoin: Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 7. Nortriptyline: Ethinyl estradiol may decrease oxidative metabolism of tricyclic antidepressants (TCAs), potentially increasing serum concentrations and adverse effects. Monitor closely. 8. Ofloxacin: Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 9. Olanzapine: Ethinyl estradiol increases olanzapine levels by affecting CYP1A2 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 10. Ombitasvir/Paritaprevir/Ritonavir with Dasabuvir: Co-administration with ethinyl estradiol is contraindicated due to the risk of significant ALT elevations. Discontinue ethinyl estradiol-containing medications before initiating this regimen and restart approximately two weeks after completing hepatitis C treatment. 11. Otesecozole: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels by inhibiting BCRP transporters. Use the lowest starting dose of BCRP substrates or reduce their dose. Monitor closely. 12. Oxcarbazepine: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 13. Paromomycin (oral): Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 14. Penicillin G and VK: Decrease ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora or increasing metabolism. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms. Use caution and monitor closely due to the risk of contraceptive failure. 15. Pentobarbital and Phenobarbital: Decrease ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 16. Phenytoin: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 17. Pioglitazone: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels by an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 18. Posaconazole: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels by affecting CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 19. Primidone: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 20. Rifabutin, Rifampin, and Rifapentine: Decrease ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 21. Ritonavir: May cause significant changes in estrogen plasma levels, reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Use a non-hormonal contraceptive method. 22. Romidepsin: Decreases ethinyl estradiol effects by receptor binding competition. Use caution and monitor closely. 23. Ropinirole: Ethinyl estradiol increases ropinirole levels by affecting CYP1A2 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 24. Rosuvastatin: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels by an unspecified mechanism. Monitor closely. 25. Rucaparib: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Adjust CYP3A4 substrate dosages if clinically indicated. 26. Rufinamide: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via weak CYP3A4 induction. Use caution and monitor closely. 27. Selegiline: Ethinyl estradiol increases selegiline levels by inhibiting N-demethylation. Use caution and monitor closely. 28. Siltuximab: May restore CYP450 enzymatic activity by inhibiting IL-6. Use caution when co-administered with narrow therapeutic index CYP substrates. 29. Somapacitan, Somatrogon, and Somatropin: Oral estrogens may reduce IGF-1 response to growth hormone analogs, potentially requiring higher GH doses. Monitor closely. 30. St. John’s Wort: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 31. Sugammadex: Use additional non-hormonal contraception for seven days after administration. 32. Sulfonamides (e.g., sulfadiazine, sulfamethoxazole, sulfisoxazole): Reduce ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 33. Tacrolimus: Ethinyl estradiol increases tacrolimus levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 34. Tazemetostat: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 35. Tecovirimat: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via weak CYP3A4 induction. Use caution and monitor closely. 36. Tetracycline: Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 37. Theophylline: Ethinyl estradiol increases theophylline levels via CYP1A2 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 38. Tigecycline: Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 39. Tinidazole: Ethinyl estradiol increases tinidazole levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 40. Tipranavir: May cause significant changes in estrogen plasma levels, reducing hormonal contraceptive efficacy. Use a non-hormonal contraceptive method. 41. Tizanidine: Ethinyl estradiol increases tizanidine levels via CYP1A2 metabolism. Monitor for adverse effects such as hypotension or bradycardia. 42. Tolterodine: Ethinyl estradiol increases tolterodine levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. 43. Topiramate: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Hormonal contraceptive efficacy may be reduced. Avoid or use an alternative drug, and consider non-hormonal contraceptive methods. 44. Tovorafenib: Decreases ethinyl estradiol levels via weak CYP3A4 induction. Avoid co-administration with hormonal contraceptives. If unavoidable, use additional non-hormonal contraception during and for 28 days after discontinuation. 45. Tranexamic Acid: Co-administration with combination hormonal contraceptives is contraindicated due to increased thrombotic risk. 46. Trazodone: Ethinyl estradiol may decrease oxidative metabolism of TCAs, potentially increasing serum concentrations and adverse effects. Monitor closely. 47. Triazolam: Ethinyl estradiol may inhibit benzodiazepine clearance, increasing serum concentrations. Use caution and monitor closely. 48. Trimethoprim: Reduces ethinyl estradiol levels by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral hormonal forms and carries a low risk of contraceptive failure. Use caution and monitor closely. 49. Tucatinib: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Avoid co-administration with CYP3A substrates due to potential toxicity. 50. Ursodiol: Ethinyl estradiol decreases ursodiol effects by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 51. Vadadustat: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels by an unspecified mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. 52. Valoctocogene Roxaparvovec: May potentiate hepatotoxicity when combined with medications that cause liver enzyme elevations. Monitor closely and consider alternative medications. 53. Valproic Acid: Ethinyl estradiol increases valproic acid elimination, potentially leading to increased seizure frequency. Modify therapy and monitor closely. 54. Voriconazole: Increases ethinyl estradiol levels via CYP3A4 metabolism. Use caution and monitor closely. Common adverse effects of ethinyl estradiol include edema, weight changes, nausea, vomiting, headache, dizziness, depression, and menstrual irregularities. Serious risks include thromboembolic events, liver dysfunction, and estrogen-dependent neoplasia. Contraindications include active or history of breast cancer, arterial thromboembolic disease, uncontrolled hypertension, and undiagnosed abnormal vaginal bleeding.
